title: Windows Kernel Driver Development
tagline: How Windows works underneath, and how drivers are built, tested and debugged safely
description: An educational course on the Windows kernel and the Windows Driver Kit, done entirely in a virtual machine: kernel architecture, a safe lab with kernel debugging, the I/O model, IOCTLs and a user-mode client, kernel memory, IRQLs and locks, DPCs and work items, observing the system through documented notifications, Driver Verifier, static analysis, secure driver design and signing. The drivers you write only echo, count and log; nothing here touches other programs. It assumes the C++ course and the Win32 API course. You build and run the drivers in a virtual machine; the practice on the site checks the logic inside them.

milestones.title: Into the Kernel
milestones.blurb: User mode and kernel mode, a safe virtual machine lab with a kernel debugger, the Windows Driver Kit, a first driver, and WinDbg.

lessons.title: User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
lessons.summary: What the kernel is, why the processor separates user mode from kernel mode, what drivers are for, and why a bug in a driver takes the whole machine down. This lesson also sets the rules for the course - everything happens in a virtual machine.

lessons.title: Building a Safe Lab
lessons.summary: Setting up the virtual machine where every driver in this course runs - Hyper-V or VMware, snapshots, test signing inside the VM only, kernel debugging over the network with KDNET, and a routine that makes crashes cheap.

lessons.title: The Windows Driver Kit
lessons.summary: Installing Visual Studio with the Windows Driver Kit, creating a driver project, what is different about building a driver, the kernel's types and calling conventions, and the kernel's string type UNICODE_STRING.

lessons.title: A First Driver
lessons.summary: The smallest driver - DriverEntry and an Unload routine that frees everything - printing with DbgPrintEx, loading and unloading it as a service with sc.exe, and what happens to each step inside the kernel.

lessons.title: Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
lessons.summary: Using WinDbg on the VM - breaking in, symbols, breakpoints in your driver, inspecting structures, reading a bug check with !analyze, and the handful of commands you will use every day.

milestones.title: The I/O Model
milestones.blurb: Device objects and symbolic links, IRPs and dispatch routines, IOCTLs with a user-mode client, buffering methods, and validating everything that comes from user mode.

lessons.title: Device Objects and Symbolic Links
lessons.summary: A driver is reached through a device object. This lesson creates one with IoCreateDevice, gives it a symbolic link so user mode can open it as \\.\XenonEcho, secures it so only administrators can, and deletes both in Unload.

lessons.title: IRPs and Dispatch Routines
lessons.summary: Every request to a driver arrives as an IRP - an I/O request packet. This lesson explains what an IRP holds, the stack locations, dispatch routines for create, close, read and write, completing a request, and why every IRP must be completed exactly once.

lessons.title: IOCTLs and a User-Mode Client
lessons.summary: Device I/O controls are a driver's private API. This lesson defines control codes with CTL_CODE, shares them in a header between driver and client, handles IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL, and writes the user-mode client that calls DeviceIoControl.

lessons.title: Buffered, Direct and Neither I/O
lessons.summary: The three ways user buffers reach a driver - the I/O manager copying through a system buffer, locking the user's pages with an MDL, or handing over raw user addresses - with their costs, their rules, and why METHOD_NEITHER is best avoided.

lessons.title: Validating Everything From User Mode
lessons.summary: A driver is a door into the kernel, and everything coming through it must be treated as hostile. This lesson lists the checks every request needs - lengths, alignment, structure versions, counts and offsets, integer overflow - and how to write handlers that cannot be tricked.

tasks.title: A request that cannot be tricked

milestones.title: Memory and Concurrency
milestones.blurb: Kernel memory and pool tags, IRQLs, spin locks and other locks, DPCs, timers and work items, and the kernel's linked lists.

lessons.title: Kernel Memory: Pools and Tags
lessons.summary: Drivers allocate from the kernel's pools - paged and non-paged - with ExAllocatePool2, tag every allocation, free everything they allocate, and use tags and PoolMon to find leaks. This lesson also defines operator new and delete for kernel C++.

tasks.title: Pool tags and a leak tracker

lessons.title: IRQL
lessons.summary: The interrupt request level decides what kernel code may do at each moment. This lesson explains PASSIVE, APC, DISPATCH and device levels, what is forbidden at each, how the documentation states each function's IRQL, and how to raise and lower it correctly.

lessons.title: Locks in the Kernel
lessons.summary: Protecting shared data in a driver - interlocked operations, spin locks and queued spin locks, fast mutexes, executive resources for many readers, and how IRQL decides which lock you may use. This lesson also covers deadlocks and lock ordering in the kernel.

lessons.title: DPCs, Timers and Work Items
lessons.summary: Deferring work in the kernel - DPCs run soon at DISPATCH_LEVEL, kernel timers fire DPCs once or periodically, and work items move work back to PASSIVE_LEVEL in a system thread. This lesson also covers making sure all of them are finished before Unload.

lessons.title: Lists in the Kernel
lessons.summary: The kernel's own data structures - intrusive doubly linked lists with LIST_ENTRY and CONTAINING_RECORD, singly linked lists, interlocked lists, lookaside lists for fixed-size allocations, and ring buffers for logs.

milestones.title: Observing the System
milestones.blurb: Documented process and thread notifications, logging and tracing from a driver, and the design of a log driver with a user-mode viewer.

lessons.title: Process and Thread Notifications
lessons.summary: Windows lets drivers observe system events through documented callbacks - process creation and exit, thread creation and exit, and image loads. This lesson registers them, explains the context they run in and what information they carry, and keeps the course's log driver strictly an observer.

lessons.title: Logging and Tracing from a Driver
lessons.summary: Getting information out of a driver without slowing the system down - DbgPrintEx levels and filters, rate limiting, WPP software tracing, and TraceLogging with ETW, which lets tools like WPR and WPA record a driver's events alongside the rest of the system.

lessons.title: Designing a Log Driver
lessons.summary: Putting milestones 2 to 4 together - the XenonLog driver records process and thread events into a ring buffer, a secured device offers one read IOCTL, and a user-mode viewer polls it, resumes where it stopped and shows what was lost. This lesson is the design, the protocol and the order to build it.

milestones.title: Quality, Security and Shipping
milestones.blurb: Driver Verifier, static analysis, secure driver design, and how drivers are signed and distributed - and when not to write one.

lessons.title: Driver Verifier
lessons.summary: Driver Verifier makes hidden driver bugs crash immediately and explain themselves - special pool for overruns and use-after-free, forced IRQL checking, pool tracking for leaks, I/O verification, deadlock detection and low-resources simulation. This lesson turns it on in the VM and reads what it reports.

lessons.title: Static Analysis and Testing
lessons.summary: Finding driver bugs before they run - SAL annotations, Code Analysis for drivers, CodeQL with Microsoft's driver queries, the Static Driver Verifier idea, unit-testing driver logic in user mode, and fuzzing IOCTL handlers.

lessons.title: Secure Driver Design
lessons.summary: Drivers run with full kernel privilege, so a flaw in one is a flaw in the whole system. This lesson lists the classic driver vulnerabilities - unprotected devices, unchecked buffers, METHOD_NEITHER, arbitrary memory access interfaces, information leaks, missing access checks - and the design rules that prevent them.

lessons.title: Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
lessons.summary: How real drivers reach users - driver packages, INF files and catalogs, Microsoft's attestation and HLK signing through the Partner Center, Windows Update - and the alternatives that make most drivers unnecessary: user-mode services, ETW, UMDF and existing system features.
